questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
{f}_{x}(x,y)=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+a{y}^{2},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=bx\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+6xy.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+a{y}^{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-2yx\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+2ay \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(bx\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+6xy) \\  & =b\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-bxy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+6y\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-2yx\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+2ay & =b\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-bxy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+6y.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $y$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy),$ respectively, we see that $a=3$ and $b=2.$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =a{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+5{y}^{2}-3, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =b{x}^{3}y+10xy, \\ {f}_{x}(2,1) & =14.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(a{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+5{y}^{2}-3) \\  & =2a{x}^{2}y+10y-0 \\  & =2a{x}^{2}y+10y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(b{x}^{3}y+10xy) \\  & =3b{x}^{2}y+10y\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}2a{x}^{2}y+10y & =3b{x}^{2}y+10y.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of ${x}^{2}y,$ we get $b=\frac{2}{3}a.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{x}(2,1)=14$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,1) & =14 \\ a(2)^{2}(1)^{2}+5(1)^{2}-3 & =14 \\ 4a+2 & =14 \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $b=\frac{2}{3}a=\frac{2}{3}(3)=2.$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=-2y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}}$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2})$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2})$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\sqrt{x}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}})=-4y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y{e}^{2x+{y}^{2}})=-4y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}))=4y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}) \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}))=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-{y}^{2})+4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x})=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Evaluate ${f}_{xyz}(4,1,7)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{xz}(x,y,z)=2x\sqrt{z-3y}+z{e}^{x-4y}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{xzy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{xz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\sqrt{z-3y}+z{e}^{x-4y}) \\  & =2x\cdot (-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{z-3y}})-4z{e}^{x-4y} \\  & =-\frac{3x}{\sqrt{z-3y}}-4z{e}^{x-4y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(4,1,7):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(4,1,7) & =-\frac{3\cdot 4}{\sqrt{7-3\cdot 1}}-4\cdot 7\cdot {e}^{4-4\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{12}{\sqrt{7-3}}-28{e}^{4-4} \\  & =-6-28 \\  & =-34\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yzx}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{xyz}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x-y+z}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-y+z}}-\frac{1}{x+y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yzx}(2,1,3) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2-1+3}}-\frac{1}{2+1+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}-\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b,$ if 

$$
f_x(x,y) = 6xy+axy^3-5, \qquad
f_y(x,y) = 3x^2+bx^2y^2, \qquad
f_y(2,-1) = -24.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we compute the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy+ax{y}^{3}-5) \\  & =6x+3ax{y}^{2}-0 \\  & =6x+3ax{y}^{2} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+b{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =6x+2bx{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. So, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & ={f}_{yx}(x,y) \\ 6x+3ax{y}^{2} & =6x+2bx{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $xy^2,$ we see that $3a=2b.$ 

Now, since $f_y(2,-1)=-24,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,-1) & =-24 \\ 3(2)^{2}+b(2)^{2}(-1)^{2} & =-24 \\ 12+4b & =-24 \\ 4b & =-36 \\ b & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}3a & =2b \\ 3a & =2(-9) \\ 3a & =-18 \\ a & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-6$ and $b=-9.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. $f_x(x,y)=x+2y$ and $f_y(x,y)=2y-x$

II. $f_x(x,y)=5(x+y)^4$ and $f_y(x,y)=5(x+y)^4$

III. $f_x(x,y)=-\sin{x}\sin{y}$ and $f_y(x,y)=\cos{x}\cos{y}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is,

$$
f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).
$$

Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, the mixed partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+2y)=2, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_{xy}(x,y) \neq f_{yx}(x,y),$ the first pair could *not* represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, the mixed partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5(x+y)^{4})=20(x+y)^{3}, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5(x+y)^{4})=20(x+y)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y),$ the second pair *could* represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, the mixed partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y),$  the third pair *could* represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y,z).$ Given that all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z\partial x} = -e^xy\sin{(yz)},
$$

 

evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,\pi,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial z\partial x\partial z}+ \dfrac{\partial^3 f }{\partial x \partial z \partial y}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂z∂x} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-{e}^{x}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-{e}^{x}{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz).\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{x}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)-{e}^{x}yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz) \\  & =-{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)+yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,\pi,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =-{e}^{(1)}(\pi )^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)=e{\pi }^{2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =-{e}^{(1)}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)+(\pi )(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1))=e\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =e{\pi }^{2}+e\pi =e\pi (\pi +1).\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y) = x y^2 - x^3 y.$ Then the first-order partial derivatives are

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (x,y) = y^2 -3x^2y \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y) = 2xy -x^3,
$$

and the second-order **mixed partial derivatives** are 

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}(x,y) = 2y -3x^2 \quad \mathrm{and} \quad  \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}(x,y) = 2y-3x^2.
$$

Notice that these two mixed partial derivatives are equal, i.e., 

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}=\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}.
$$

In general, if a function $f(x,y)$ has continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U,$ and the second-order mixed partial derivatives exist and are continuous on $U,$ then the mixed partial derivatives are equal everywhere on $U.$

tutorials.name: Equality of Higher-Order Partial Derivatives
tutorials.problem:
If $f(x,y)$ is a function whose first-order and second-order mixed partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ then the second-order mixed partial derivatives are equal everywhere on $U.$

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y} =\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}
$$

This result also extends to higher-order partial derivatives. For example, if the third-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ are also continuous everywhere on $U,$ then the third-order mixed partial derivatives are independent of the order in which the differentiation is performed. 

For example,

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} =\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{red}\partial y\, \partial x \, \partial x}.
$$

In this case, we can think of $\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y$ and $\color{red}\partial y\, \partial x \, \partial x$ as distinct permutations of the symbols $\partial x,\partial x,$ and $\partial y.$ Any permutation of these symbols gives the same result. For example,

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} = \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{purple}\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial x}.
$$

**Watch out!** This does **not** mean that *all* third partial derivatives are equal! For example, it is generally true that

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} \neq \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial y}.
$$

 
These are not equal because $\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial y$ (in the right-hand side denominator) is a permutation of the symbols $\partial x, \partial y, \partial y,$ not $\partial x, \partial x, \partial y.$
tutorials.title: Equality of Higher-Order Partial Derivatives
tutorials.content:
If $f(x,y)$ is a function whose first-order and second-order mixed partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ then the second-order mixed partial derivatives are equal everywhere on $U.$

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y} =\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}
$$

This result also extends to higher-order partial derivatives. For example, if the third-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ are also continuous everywhere on $U,$ then the third-order mixed partial derivatives are independent of the order in which the differentiation is performed. 

For example,

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} =\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{red}\partial y\, \partial x \, \partial x}.
$$

In this case, we can think of $\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y$ and $\color{red}\partial y\, \partial x \, \partial x$ as distinct permutations of the symbols $\partial x,\partial x,$ and $\partial y.$ Any permutation of these symbols gives the same result. For example,

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} = \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{purple}\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial x}.
$$

**Watch out!** This does **not** mean that *all* third partial derivatives are equal! For example, it is generally true that

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\color{blue}\partial x\, \partial x\, \partial y} \neq \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial y}.
$$

 
These are not equal because $\partial x\, \partial y\, \partial y$ (in the right-hand side denominator) is a permutation of the symbols $\partial x, \partial y, \partial y,$ not $\partial x, \partial x, \partial y.$
